history_of_present_illness: Amoebic dysentery is the clinical manifestation. Details on symptom progression and other clinical features are not provided.
exposure_and_epidemiology: The definitive host is man. The important reservoir is man in the carrier stage, shedding cysts in feces. Transmission occurs through ingestion of cysts present in contaminated food or water. Flies may also act as mechanical carriers.

rows: Cysts in food or water. Flies may act as carriers. Ingestive. Amoebic dysentery.
Transmission probably same as for E. histolytica. Found in those having care of hogs. Ingestive. Balantidium dysentery. Anaemia.
Transmission probably same as for E. histolytica. Rat feces on human food important. Ingestive. Lamblia dysentery. Giardiasis.
Cyclical development in louse. Bite puncture contaminated by crushed louse. Relapsing fever.

T. pallidum. Usually venereal. Syphilis. T. pertenue. Flies or contact. Yaws.
Common infection of rats. Present in blood. Excreted in urine. Ingestion. Weil’s disease.

rows: Not definitely known. Eating raw fish. Ingestive. Human liver fluke disease.

Possibly 1st, mollusc. Cercariae encyst on grass.
Eating raw crabs containing cercariae. Ingestive. Lung fluke disease.
Bathing or drinking water containing cercariae. Penetrative. Vesical bilharziasis.

tables.title: Helminthic Diseases (Continued). Nematodes
rows: Indirect in mosquito. Mature larva penetrates skin. Elephantiasis, etc.
Probably indirect (cyclical) in Chrysops. Probably inoculative. Ocular filariasis, etc.
Transmission by mosquitoes and ticks suggested. No pathogenicity.
Larvae enter cyclops. Infected cyclops in drinking water. Ingestive. Guinea worm infection.
Possibly Glossina. Subcutaneous tumor and lymphangitis.
Parasitic filariform larva penetrates skin. Pathogenicity doubtful.
Encysted strongyloid larvae penetrate skin. Ancylostomiasis.
Encysted larva in raw or insufficiently cooked pork. Ingestive. Trichinosis.

tables.title: Helminthic Diseases. Cestodes
rows: Eating raw fish containing pleocercoid larvae. Broad Russian tapeworm disease.
Man intermediate and definitive host. Ingestive. Dwarf tapeworm disease.
Eating insufficiently cooked beef containing cysticerci. Ingestive. Beef tapeworm disease.
Eating insufficiently cooked pork containing cysticerci. Ingestion. Pork tapeworm disease.
Dogs infected at abattoir. Hydatid disease.

tables.title: Arthropodan Diseases
rows: Adult in nasal cavity of dogs, etc. Eggs in nasal mucus contaminate grass. Rabbits, cattle infected. Larvae in liver, lungs.
Porocephaliasis. Man may harbor adult or larva. Larvae usually in lungs or liver and do not seem to cause symptoms.
Adults in lungs of snakes. Eggs contaminate water or food. Larvae in liver, lungs, etc., of lions, monkeys, man, etc.
Porocephaliasis. Larvae wander in abdominal cavity or lungs in which latter they produce a chronic bronchitis which may resemble phthisis.
All stages passed within hair follicles or sebaceous cysts especially about nose. Adult may wander.
Demodectic acariasis. Causes a resistant itch in dogs. In man, may invade eyelids or meibomian glands, and has been reported as causing various forms of dermatitis.
Female lives in burrow of skin giving off eggs which hatch into larvae.
Scabies. Burrows show as blackish lines, especially between fingers, flexor surfaces of arms and penis. Itching worse at night.
Female lives on wheat straw worm or grain moth. Larval mites develop inside mother.

Grain itch. The mites leave wheat straw or grain and attack harvesters or those sleeping on straw mattresses. Attack upper trunk, neck and arms. Erythematous or vesicular eruption with constitutional symptoms.
Adults live in fields or woods. The larval mite lives on grasshoppers or small rodents.
Autumnal erythema. The larval mites known as red bug or jigger attack man causing a severe itch.
Mites live in chicken houses and feed on fowls.
Poultryman’s itch. The mites attack man producing eczematous dermatitis on backs of hands and forearms.
Adults live on cattle, sheep, etc. May bite man.
Tick paralysis. The bite of this tick or Ixodes holocyclus may produce paralysis in sheep. An ascending type of paralysis due to tick bites has been several times noted in man, chiefly in children.
Adults live on clothing or hair and feed on man.
Pediculosis—Phthiriasis. Produce skin irritation with later on pigmentation (Vagabondismus).
Impregnated female penetrates skin of man or animals, especially toes and feet.
Sandflea or chigoe infestation. Site of penetration shows as black spot with whitish induration surrounding it. Apt to form ulcers.

tables.title: Arthropodan Diseases (Continued)
rows: Eggs of fly become attached to mosquitoes or ticks. These latter bite man and larva penetrates skin.
A cutaneous myiasis. Larva at first club shaped (ver macaque), later worm shaped (torcel). Larva causes a swelling with black opening. May invade eye.
Larvae of this or other flies burrow under skin.
Creeping eruption. Larva migrans. The burrows make zig-zag lines on face or soles of feet. Causes itching.
Chrysomyia macellaria, and C. dux Muscidae). Oestrus ovis (Oestridae).
Fly deposits eggs in nostrils. Larvae wander to nasal sinuses. May invade aural canal.

Screw worm infection. Nasal myiasis. Larvae in their wandering destroy tissues of nasal cavities, or of ear, and may cause death. May infest wounds or vagina. C. macellaria causes American nasal myiasis, C. dux causes Indian nasal myiasis and O. ovis causes African nasal myiasis.
An African fly, which deposits eggs on children and animals.
Larvae bore under skin, causing boil-like lesions with central opening. Larvae mature in two weeks.
An African fly deposits eggs on floors of native huts. Larvae bite man.
Congo floor maggot. The bite is not painful.
Calliphora vomitoria and Lucilia caesar and L. serricata (Muscidae).
Blow and bluebottle flies, depositing eggs on tainted meats. Larvae may be found in feces.
Larvae may be cause of obscure abdominal conditions; may be found in nasal cavities, causing serious symptoms, or in ear.
Eggs presumably deposited near genitalia or ear.
Larvae have been found in male urethra and in the ear.
Viviparous. Larvae are deposited on decaying flesh (wounds, orifices of body).
Larvae gain access to wounds, nasal cavities, etc., at times causing death. Commonly found in intestinal myiases. May occur in vagina.
Occasionally reported as found in ear.
Eggs deposited near external genitalia and larva penetrates urethra.
Symptoms of urinary irritation or obstruction. Has been found in gastro-intestinal tract.
